opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the partnerships are really central to how we think about the long-term trajectory of the models. When we work with a pharma or biotech partner, we're not just handing over a tool and walking away. We're getting embedded in real drug discovery programs, on targets people genuinely care about, and that exposes the models to the kinds of problems that never show up in public benchmarks.

A lot of the public data in structural biology and antibody design is skewed. It's what people chose to crystallize or publish, which is often the successes and the easy cases. Partners bring the hard targets, the weird epitopes, the molecules that failed for reasons nobody wrote down. Seeing where the model works and where it breaks in that setting is incredibly valuable signal for us.

There's also the lab loop. Our models make designs, those designs get synthesized and tested, and the experimental results tell us something very concrete about where the model's sense of physics or binding is off. Over many programs that becomes a feedback loop that's really hard to replicate any other way. We're very careful about respecting partner data and IP, but even the learnings at the level of "the model is overconfident in this regime" or "this class of targets needs a different approach" shape what we build next.

And then partners keep us honest about what actually matters. It's easy in AI to optimize a metric that looks great on paper. Drug hunters care whether the molecule is developable, whether it hits the right epitope, whether it'll survive the next ten steps of the pipeline. Having those people as close collaborators pulls our research toward the things that move programs forward, and I think over time that's what makes the models genuinely better rather than just better on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says partnerships steer research toward outcomes drug hunters value, such as developability and advancing programs, and that this makes the models better over time.

r002.rationale: It describes models generating designs that partners synthesize and test, with experimental results feeding back into later model development across programs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people sometimes miss about what we're doing at Chai is that the model isn't the product, at least not in the way a chatbot is a product. The model is the engine, but the real test of whether it's any good happens in a wet lab, not on a benchmark. And that's where the partnership model becomes essential rather than just a business decision.

When we work with a partner on a real target, we get something you can't get from public data: ground truth on the hard cases. PDB is incredible, but it's biased toward things that crystallize nicely and toward targets people have cared about for thirty years. The molecules our partners actually need are usually the ones that aren't in that distribution. Novel targets, difficult epitopes, things where there's no homolog to lean on. Every time we design something for a partner and it gets synthesized and tested, we learn where the model is confident and wrong, which is the most valuable kind of signal there is.

So the feedback loop looks like this: we generate designs, the partner tests them, we get back binding data, expression data, sometimes structural data, and all of that flows back into how we think about the next version. Not always as raw training data, because a lot of it is confidential and stays that way, but as evaluation. It tells us which failure modes matter in the real world versus which ones only matter on a leaderboard. That shapes what we prioritize, what we ablate, what we decide is worth a six-month research push.

The other piece is that partners push us toward generalization in a way we wouldn't push ourselves. If you only optimize for one assay or one target class, you get a model that's great at that one thing. When you've got a dozen partners across different modalities, antibodies, small molecules, peptides, you're forced to build something that actually understands the underlying physics and biology, because there's no shortcut that works across all of them. Honestly, that pressure has made the models better faster than I think we'd have gotten to on our own.

And then longer term, the ambition is that this compounds. Each program raises the floor on what the next program starts with. If we do this right, in a few years the model has seen the outcomes of hundreds of real design campaigns, and at that point it's learning from something that looks a lot more like actual drug discovery than anything in the public literature. That's the version of this that I think really changes the field.

r001.rationale: The response says partner testing helps improve models, but it does not clearly identify aligned incentives between model improvement and better customer outcomes.

r002.rationale: It describes Chai generating designs for partners, partners testing them and returning data, and that feedback shaping subsequent model versions and future programs.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is creating a feedback loop between our models and real-world experiments. A partner brings a problem they care about, we design molecules, and then experimental testing tells us which predictions actually hold up. Those results can help us understand where the models are strong and where they need to improve.

Over time, working across different problems can make that feedback much more valuable. The goal is for better models to lead to better experimental outcomes, and for what we learn from those experiments to inform the next generation of models. That’s what can make a partnership valuable well beyond any single project.

r001.rationale: The response connects partnerships with better experimental outcomes, but does not clearly say that the model improvement incentives are aligned with better outcomes for customers.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop: better models lead to better experimental outcomes, and experimental results inform the next generation of models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the long-term opportunity is to create a feedback loop between the models and real experimental work. A partnership can help us understand what people actually need to design, where our predictions are useful, and where they fall short. Those lessons can guide the next generation of models.

The key is making that valuable for both sides: partners make progress on their programs, and, where our agreements allow, we learn from experimental feedback. Over time, that can help us build models that are more useful in practice, with a better understanding of when to trust their predictions.

r001.rationale: It says the partnership should be valuable for both sides: partners make progress on their programs while experimental feedback helps improve future models.

r002.rationale: It describes experimental feedback improving later models, but does not say better models enable new data generation.
